w: A synagogue and a mosque stand right beside each other on this street - Neveh Shalom and the Ahmadiyya mosque - often cited as a symbol of Suriname's religious coexistence. Commercial near the river, it turns residential further out, renamed Verlengde Keizerstraat, before ending near a cluster of cemeteries.
s: A synagogue and a mosque, side by side
_facts: Best known for the adjacent Neveh Shalom Synagogue and Ahmadiyya Anjuman Isha'at Islam Mosque
Their proximity is often read as a symbol of Suriname's religious coexistence
Commercial near the Suriname River, turning residential and renamed Verlengde Keizerstraat further out
Ends near a cluster of cemeteries; also home to a police bureau, a mall and a McDonald's

w: A wooden fort raised by the French in 1640 was seized and reinforced by the British as Fort Willoughby, then captured by the Dutch in 1667 and renamed Fort Zeelandia. Its changing flags trace the tug-of-war between the two colonial powers that ended only with the Treaty of Breda.
s: A fort that changed hands three times
_facts: Built as a wooden fort by the French in 1640
Reinforced by the British and renamed Fort Willoughby during their colonial period
Taken by the Dutch in 1667 and renamed Fort Zeelandia
Control of Paramaribo switched between Dutch and British until the Treaty of Breda ceded Suriname to the Dutch

w: Officially the Ahmadiyya Anjuman Isha'at Islam Mosque, this is the headquarters of the Lahore Ahmadiyya Movement in Suriname - and it stands directly next to the Neveh Shalom Synagogue. The pairing is one of the few places anywhere with a mosque and synagogue sharing a boundary wall.
s: A mosque headquarters, wall to wall with a synagogue
_facts: Officially the Ahmadiyya Anjuman Isha'at Islam Mosque Keizerstraat
Headquarters of the Lahore Ahmadiyya Movement (Surinaamse Islamitische Vereniging) in Suriname
Situated directly adjacent to the Neveh Shalom Synagogue on Keizerstraat

w: Built by the Arya Diwaker association, this is the largest Hindu mandir in Suriname, standing in open fields near the city centre. It draws visitors well beyond the Hindu community, arriving from across Suriname and from abroad to see the country's biggest temple.
_facts: A Hindu association, Arya Diwaker, built Suriname's biggest mandir (Hindu temple)
Located in fields in the Paramaribo city centre
Attracts both Hindu and non-Hindu visitors from Suriname and abroad

w: Royal palms behind the Presidential Palace were planted on the order of governor Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck, who opened the garden to the public in 1685 - then was murdered by mutinous soldiers in 1688, closing it for two centuries. Capuchin monkeys still roam among the palms today.
s: A palm garden opened, then closed by murder
_facts: Royal palms planted from 1683-1688 on the order of governor Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck, who opened the garden to the public in 1685
The governor was murdered by mutinous soldiers in 1688; the garden then closed until the early 20th century
Home to tall royal palms, tropical birds and troops of capuchin monkeys, behind the Presidential Palace
Cited specifically when Paramaribo's historic centre joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2002; UNESCO funded a 2009 refurbishment

w: The second-largest church in Paramaribo, this Roman Catholic building - also called the Santa Rosa Church - was rebuilt in 1911 and stands within the UNESCO-listed historic centre, among the colonial-era buildings that earned the city's core its World Heritage status.
_facts: Roman Catholic church, known in Dutch as Sint Rosakerk
Current building dates from 1911
Second-largest church in Paramaribo
Located in the city centre, within the UNESCO World Heritage historic centre

w: In January 2017, the last Surinamese records from the Dutch colonial period were repatriated from the Netherlands, closing a project begun in 2009 - but not before the Dutch archive scanned the entire inventory, so researchers anywhere can still consult it. Britain's share stays in London.
_facts: Formed from the 1956 Landsarchiefdienst and the 1982 Staatsarchief, merged in 1989 and renamed National Archives in 2006
In January 2017, the last Surinamese archives from the Dutch colonial period were repatriated from the Netherlands
The Dutch Nationaal Archief scanned the whole inventory before repatriation so it stays available abroad
Records from the British colonial period remain in The National Archives in the UK

w: A gentlemen's club before it became an emergency seat of government: when Suriname's National Assembly building burned down on 1 August 1996, parliament moved into this former park clubhouse on Onafhankelijkheidsplein - and simply stayed.
s: A gentlemen's club turned parliament building
_facts: A park and former gentlemen's club on Onafhankelijkheidsplein
The National Assembly of Suriname's building burned down on 1 August 1996
The National Assembly relocated into this former park clubhouse afterward

w: Paramaribo's oldest street runs along the Suriname River from Onafhankelijkheidsplein to the Central Market - exactly where ships once docked to unload. Its riverside buildings, in the historic centre, earned the strip a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2002.
s: The riverfront street where ships once docked
_facts: The oldest and one of the most important streets in Paramaribo
Runs along the Suriname River, where ships used to arrive
Extends from Onafhankelijkheidsplein to the Central Market
Designated part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002

w: This former weigh house on the Waterkant once tallied goods off every arriving ship before sale. Long retired from weighing anything, the Waag survives as a protected monument within Paramaribo's UNESCO-listed historic centre.
s: The old weigh house on the waterfront
_facts: A former weigh house on the Waterkant in the historic centre
The building is a protected monument
Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site

w: Home of Elisabeth Samson, the first Afro-Surinamese millionaire, this Wagenwegstraat house passed to the State after her death and sat neglected by the early 2000s. Novelist Cynthia McLeod campaigned for its rescue, and the Elisabeth Samson Foundation bought it on 19 January 2021, planning to turn it into a museum.
s: The house of Suriname's first Black millionaire
_facts: Former home of Elisabeth Samson, the first Afro-Surinamese millionaire
Bought by the State after her death; neglected by the early 21st century
Novelist Cynthia McLeod campaigned for its restoration
Bought by the Elisabeth Samson Foundation on 19 January 2021, to become a museum

w: Built during the Second World War to barrack American troops stationed in Suriname, this compound has been renamed twice since: Prins Bernhard kampement in 1950, then Memre Boekoe after independence in 1975, honouring a fort from the Boni Wars. It still serves as headquarters of the Surinamese Land Forces.
_facts: Built in World War II as barracks for American soldiers stationed in Suriname, originally Kampement Gemenelandsweg
Renamed Prins Bernhard kampement in 1950
Renamed Memre Boekoe barracks after independence in 1975, after Fort Boekoe from the Boni Wars
Currently headquarters of the Surinamese Land Forces

w: Sculptor Jozef Klas cast this statue, named Kwakoe, to commemorate the abolition of slavery in Suriname. It stands in central Paramaribo as one of the city's monuments dedicated specifically to that history.
s: A statue marking the end of slavery
_facts: A statue in Paramaribo commemorating the abolition of slavery
Made by sculptor Jozef Klas

w: The first Lutheran church on this Waterkant site burned down in 1832; its replacement, standing since 1834, still serves the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Suriname and carries protected-monument status within the historic centre.
s: A Lutheran church rebuilt after fire
_facts: Church of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Suriname, on Waterkant in the historic centre
The first church on the site burned down in 1832
The current building dates from 1834 and is a protected monument

w: Two floors trade side by side at Paramaribo's Centrale Markt on the Waterkant: fruit, vegetables, meat and fish on the ground floor, clothing, cigarettes and CDs upstairs. It sits directly on the bank of the Suriname River and opens six days a week, Monday to Saturday.
s: Food below, clothes and CDs above
_facts: A two-floor marketplace on the Waterkant, on the Suriname River
Ground floor sells fruit, vegetables, meat and fish
Top floor sells clothing, cigarettes, CDs and other consumer goods
Open Monday to Saturday

w: Known in Sranan Tongo as Mamakerki, the Grote Stadskerk on Steenbakkerijstraat was the first Moravian church built in Suriname and remains the largest congregation of the Moravian Church in the country. The building carries protected-monument status within the historic centre.
s: Suriname's first and largest Moravian church
_facts: Known in Sranan Tongo as Mamakerki
First Moravian church built in Suriname
Remains the largest congregation of the Moravian Church in Suriname
Located on Steenbakkerijstraat in the historic centre; a protected monument
